a: Now I myself, Paul
t: A new tone: one letter or two?
p: Chapters 10 to 13 sound different from 1 to 9, and scholars disagree about why.
b: In chapters 1 to 9 Paul is relieved and warm (7:5-16). From 10:1 he is sharp and sarcastic. Four explanations are common. One letter: Paul had good news about the majority, and now turns to a stubborn minority who still follow his rivals (Harris, Garland, Barnett). Two letters, with 10 to 13 first: these chapters are the "severe letter" of 2:3-4 and 7:8, a theory first argued in detail by Adolf Hausrath in 1870. Two letters, with 10 to 13 last: new bad news reached Paul after chapter 9 was written. Margaret Thrall, in her International Critical Commentary, takes this view: chapters 10 to 13 are a separate letter written after chapters 1 to 9, and she rejects the identification with the severe letter. No surviving Greek manuscript puts chapters 10 to 13 anywhere but here. Against the "severe letter" idea, the wrongdoer of 2:5-11 and 7:12 is never mentioned in 10 to 13.

a: by the meekness and gentleness of Christ
p: Paul bases his appeal on the character of Christ, the very quality his critics call weakness.
b: Praütes ("meekness") means strength held under control, the word Jesus uses of himself (Matthew 11:29). Epieikeia ("gentleness") is a willingness not to insist on one's full rights. Paul does not mean he will be soft: the next verses promise a hard line. He means that if he must be hard, it will be Christ's way, not the way of a bully. Some copyists spelled the first word differently (praütēs or prautēs), which makes no difference in English.

a: "humble"
p: To a Greek ear, being humble often meant being low class and weak, not modest.
b: The word tapeinos was usually used in the Greek world for something low, small or servile; it was seldom a compliment, though not every Greek writer used it that way. The word is probably quoted from Paul's critics ("humble in person, but bold from a distance"). Paul takes the insult and wears it: he says he "made himself low" for the Corinthians (11:7), and that God may "humble" him over their sins (12:21). Jesus in Philippians 2:8 "humbled himself" in the same way.

a: "according to the flesh."
p: The charge is that Paul acts by merely human motives, not that he sins with his body.
b: Here "flesh" means the human, unspiritual level: self-interest, ambition, calculation. Earlier, some in Corinth had said Paul changed his travel plans "according to the flesh", meaning he said yes and no as it suited him (1:17). The charge is that his authority is only talk and his motives are worldly. Paul answers in 10:3 with a wordplay: he does live "in" the flesh (he has a human body and a human life), but he does not fight "according to" it.

a: Before God they have the power to tear down strongholds.
p: The Greek can mean powerful before God, by God, or very powerful.
b: The phrase dynata tō theō uses a dative that is hard to pin down. It can mean "powerful for God" (in his service), "powerful in God's sight", "powerful by God's help", or, as an old idiom, simply "extremely powerful". The word for "strongholds" (ochyrōmata) is military. Greek philosophers also described the moral struggle as a war, and Abraham Malherbe has shown how closely Paul's language matches theirs. Paul's point is the same in every reading: his weapons are words, truth and patience, not force or flattery.
orig: δυνατὰ τῷ θεῷ πρὸς καθαίρεσιν ὀχυρωμάτων

a: We lead every thought away as a prisoner
p: In context this is about arguments against the knowledge of God, not private mental habits.
b: The verb aichmalōtizō means to take prisoners of war. Paul uses a picture of a conqueror leading captives (compare 2:14). The "thoughts" (noēmata) are the same word he uses for the "minds" of the Corinthians that might be corrupted (11:3). So the verse is about the contest over what the Corinthians will believe about Christ, not about controlling every passing thought, which is how it is often preached. The captive thoughts are made to obey Christ, not Paul.

a: once your own obedience has been made full
p: Paul will discipline only after the loyal majority has finished the work of obedience.
b: Paul does not threaten the whole church. He plans to let the loyal majority complete their obedience first (they had already shown it, 7:15), and then deal with the rebels. This matches how Paul handled the offender in 2:5-11: the church acted, and Paul went along. The same pattern shows in 13:1-2, where he promises a fair hearing and no leniency. Church discipline by a community, not by one leader, is the model in 1 Corinthians 5:4-5.

a: sure in his own mind that he belongs to Christ
p: Some in Corinth claimed a special tie to Christ; Paul says his tie is no less.
b: Paul may be answering the rivals' slogan, or the old Corinthian slogan "I am of Christ" (1 Corinthians 1:12), or a claim that the rivals had known the earthly Jesus (compare 5:16). The Greek of the first sentence can be a statement ("you are looking at the surface"), a command ("look at what is in front of you!") or a question ("do you look only at the surface?"). All three fit. His reply is calm: if anyone is sure he belongs to Christ, he should think again, and see that Paul belongs to Christ just as he does.

a: The Lord gave it to us to build you up, not to tear you down.
p: Paul's description of his authority echoes the call of the prophet Jeremiah.
b: The pairing of "build up" and "tear down" recalls God's words to Jeremiah, who was put in charge of nations "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (Jeremiah 1:10). Paul has just used "tear down" for the strongholds (10:4) and now says his authority is mainly for building. He repeats the line at the very end of his warning (13:10), so the whole section is framed by it. "Build up" is also Paul's key word for what love does in the church (1 Corinthians 8:1; 14:12).

a: "His letters are weighty and strong," someone says,
t: A speaker who wrote better than he spoke
p: Paul's critics said he was impressive on paper and unimpressive in person.
b: In the Greek cities of the day, a public speaker was judged by his voice, his looks and his polish. The professional speakers called sophists drew crowds and fees. Paul grants that he is "untrained in speaking" (11:6) and had said at his first visit that he did not come with fine words (1 Corinthians 2:1-5). The late second-century Acts of Paul describes him as small, bald and bowlegged. It may preserve a memory or may be a caricature; it cannot be checked. Bruce Winter has argued that the Corinthians were measuring Paul against the sophists.

a: recommend themselves
p: "Recommend" is a key word in this letter: the question is who vouches for a minister.
b: The Greek synistēmi means to introduce, vouch for or recommend, and it runs through the letter (3:1; 4:2; 5:12; 6:4; 10:12, 18; 12:11). Travelling teachers carried letters of recommendation, and Paul's rivals evidently did. Paul replies that the Corinthian church is his letter (3:2-3) and that the only recommendation that counts is the Lord's (10:18). In 10:12 he says his rivals use themselves as both ruler and the thing measured, so they always win.

a: the field that God has measured out to us
p: Paul talks of a territory with limits, like a surveyor's plot; his rivals had entered it.
b: The Greek word kanōn means a measuring rod, and so a limit, and so an assigned district. Paul believes God gave him a field that includes Corinth because he was first to bring the good news there (Acts 18:1-11). He may be thinking of the agreement in Jerusalem that divided the missions between Peter to the Jews and Paul to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7-9). Elsewhere he says he avoids building "on another's foundation" (Romans 15:20). His rivals, in his view, took credit for a church they did not found.
orig: κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τοῦ κανόνος (kata to metron tou kanonos)

a: the lands beyond you
p: Paul wants Corinth's support for a mission further west.
b: When Paul wrote this, he was in Macedonia and about to go to Corinth (13:1). A few months later, from Corinth, he wrote to the Romans that he had "completed" his work from Jerusalem round to Illyricum and planned to go to Spain by way of Rome (Romans 15:19-24). So "the lands beyond you" probably means Spain, with Rome as a stop on the way (the church at Rome already existed, and Paul says he does not build on another's foundation, Romans 15:20-24). He hoped that growing faith in Corinth would give him the base and the help for that. This explains why the quarrel with the Corinthians mattered so much to him.

a: "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord."
p: Paul sums up Jeremiah 9:24; he quotes the same line in 1 Corinthians 1:31.
b: The line is a short form of Jeremiah: "If anyone is to boast, let it be in this alone" (Jeremiah 9:24), followed there by knowing the LORD. Paul gives no "it is written" here, but he quotes it with that formula in 1 Corinthians 1:31. In Jeremiah, "the LORD" is YHWH; in 10:18 the "Lord" who commends is probably Christ, as in 1 Corinthians 1:30-31, where the line follows a statement about Christ. This verse is the rule behind all the boasting of chapters 11 and 12: whatever Paul boasts of, he says he is boasting in the Lord.

a: Actually, you do bear with me.
p: The Greek can say "you do bear with me" or "do bear with me!"
b: The Greek alla kai anechesthe mou can be indicative ("indeed you do bear with me") or imperative ("do bear with me!"). The Plain takes it as a statement, since Paul goes on to say that the Corinthians put up with the rivals so readily (11:4, 19-20). Many translations take it as the command, which fits the first half of the verse, a wish that they would bear with him.

a: I am jealous for you with a jealousy that is God's own.
p: In the Bible, jealousy is the faithful love of a husband who will not share his bride.
b: In the Old Testament God is "jealous" because Israel is his bride and her loyalty belongs to him (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Hosea 2:19-20; Ezekiel 16). The Greek says "with God's jealousy", which can mean a jealousy like God's, from God, or on God's behalf. Paul presents himself as the father of the bride (he founded the church, 1 Corinthians 4:15), who guards her until the wedding. That day is when Christ comes: the church is the bride in Ephesians 5:25-27 and Revelation 19:7; 21:2. In John 3:29 the groom's friend is filled with joy at the groom's voice.
r: Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:14; Hosea 2:19-20; Ezekiel 16:8; Isaiah 54:5; John 3:29; Ephesians 5:25-27; Revelation 19:7

a: so that I could present you to Christ as a pure virgin
p: In Paul's world a betrothed girl was kept pure by her father until the wedding.
b: A Jewish or Roman engagement was binding, but the bride stayed in her father's house until the wedding. The father was responsible for her purity (Deuteronomy 22:13-21). Paul uses this to describe the church's position: promised to one husband, with the wedding still ahead. The word "present" (paristēmi) is also used of presenting the church to Christ at his coming (Ephesians 5:27; Colossians 1:22, 28). The danger is not that the church is unfaithful in body, but that its loyalty and its thoughts are turned elsewhere (11:3).

a: just as the snake fooled Eve with his cunning
p: Paul compares the Corinthians to Eve and the rivals to the serpent.
b: This echoes Genesis 3: "The snake fooled me" (Genesis 3:13). Paul's verb is a stronger form of the Greek of the Septuagint. Eve stands for the whole church, and the serpent for whoever leads them away from "simple, pure loyalty". Paul does not say what the serpent's trick was. Some Jewish writers connected the serpent with sexual seduction; 4 Maccabees 18:7-8 (a Jewish work, probably of the first century AD, printed in an appendix to some Orthodox Bibles and not Scripture for Catholics or most Protestants) has a mother say that no "deceiving serpent" spoiled the purity of her virginity. Paul's mix of "pure virgin" and "serpent" in one breath may reflect that tradition, though this is only a possible link. He speaks of Eve again only in 1 Timothy 2:13-14. In Romans 5 the blame falls on Adam.

a: "super-apostles"
p: Paul mocks a group of rivals. Scholars disagree whether they were the Jerusalem apostles or newcomers.
b: The Greek word is hyperlian apostoloi. Hyperlian is a rare, stretched adverb, "beyond the limit" or "over the top", and it is plainly sarcastic. The Plain's "super-apostles" is a coined label, not a Greek title: it tries to keep the mockery that "highest rank" would hide. Views: (1) Two groups. The "super-apostles" are the Twelve and the Jerusalem leaders, whom the intruders invoke, and Paul is mocking the Corinthians' high opinion of them; the "false apostles" of 11:13 are the intruders (Käsemann; Barrett, in his 1971 article and 1973 commentary). The strongest case for this is that 11:5 and 11:13 use two different labels, and Galatians 2:6 is itself guarded about "those who seemed to be something". (2) One group. They are the same intruders as the "false apostles" of 11:13, ironically named by their own boast. Many recent commentators take this view. (3) Who the intruders were. Jewish-Christian preachers from Judea (Barnett), Hellenistic Jewish "divine men" and miracle workers (Georgi), or spiritual enthusiasts (Schmithals, with gnostics). Against view (1), Paul speaks warmly of the Jerusalem leaders elsewhere (1 Corinthians 15:3-11; Galatians 2:9), though a guarded tone in Galatians 2:6 shows he did not hold them above question.

a: free of charge
t: Paul would not take Corinth's money
p: Accepting a gift made a person a client of the giver, so Paul's refusal looked like a snub.
b: In Corinth, status ran on patronage: whoever gave you money owned a piece of you. Paul supported himself at his trade (Acts 18:3; 1 Corinthians 4:12) and took gifts from other churches, as the Philippians' help in Macedonia shows (Philippians 4:15-16). He meant his refusal as a gift that left the gospel free. The Corinthians, however, seem to have taken it as an insult to their friendship or as a sign that he was no real teacher, since teachers who charged were thought more valuable. Peter Marshall and Ronald Hock explain this background.

a: I robbed other churches by taking wages from them
p: Paul uses the language of plunder, with a smile, for the gifts he got from Macedonia.
b: The verb sylaō means to strip or plunder, as soldiers take spoil. The noun for "wages" (opsōnion) is the pay or rations of a soldier. Paul keeps the military pictures of chapter 10. He is exaggerating: the churches gave willingly. The point is the contrast: he took from poor Macedonians (8:1-5) in order to serve rich Corinth without charge.

a: false apostles
t: "False apostles" and the test of an apostle
p: Paul's word is found only here; the early church later wrote rules for testing apostles.
b: Pseudapostoloi seems to be Paul's own coinage. He says they are "workers who cheat" (compare "evil workers" in Philippians 3:2). Revelation 2:2 says the church at Ephesus tested those who called themselves apostles and found them false. The Didache, a church manual from the late first or early second century, tells a church to receive an apostle but not to let him stay more than two days or ask for money (Didache 11:3-6). Paul's own test is different: not letters or signs alone, but the cross-shaped life and the church he founded.

a: Satan himself takes on the look of an angel of light.
p: Paul seems to know a tradition that Satan came to Eve looking like an angel.
b: The Old Testament says nothing about Satan appearing as an angel to Eve. A Jewish retelling, the Life of Adam and Eve (the Greek form is called the Apocalypse of Moses), says that Satan took the form of an angel and spoke to Eve (Life of Adam and Eve 9:1; Apocalypse of Moses 17:1). Paul may be drawing on such a tradition. It would make his link between 11:3 and 11:14 tighter: as Satan came to Eve in disguise, so now his servants come to Corinth. This is a possible background, not proven. The Life of Adam and Eve is a writing outside the 66, probably from the first centuries AD; it is in no church's Bible and was never counted as Scripture.
r: Genesis 3:1-6; 2 Corinthians 11:3; Life of Adam and Eve 9:1; Apocalypse of Moses 17:1; Matthew 7:15

a: take me for a fool
p: From here to 12:10 Paul brags in the style of a fool, and uses it to attack boasting.
b: Ancient teachers of speaking, such as Plutarch in his essay On Inoffensive Self-Praise, said self-praise is rude unless forced on you, for example by an attack. Paul follows several of those rules: he says he is forced to boast (12:11), he calls it foolish, he boasts of weakness, and he gives credit to God. Scholars compare it to Socratic irony (Betz), Hellenistic rhetoric (Forbes, Judge) and the Roman habit of listing one's honors, as in the emperor Augustus's Res Gestae. Scholars disagree how closely Paul follows the rules, since he also says he is not a trained speaker (11:6). The speech runs from 11:16 to 12:10, and the lines about folly return in 12:6 and 12:11.

a: eats you up
p: The five "if someone" lines show how the rivals treated the Corinthians.
b: The five actions are enslaving, devouring (eating up your property), grabbing (taking), lifting himself up, and slapping in the face. Some commentators take them literally: the rivals took money, ruled over the church and may even have struck people. Others take them as sarcastic exaggeration. In either case, Paul's point is that the Corinthians, who think themselves so wise (11:19), tolerate abuse from strangers while they criticized Paul for being weak, a man who never took a penny from them.

a: Are they Hebrews?
p: The rivals were Jews, and Paul claims the same Jewish pedigree without boasting that it saves.
b: Each of the three claims says something. Hebrew probably means one with a Hebrew or Aramaic background (Paul says "a Hebrew of Hebrews" in Philippians 3:5; compare Acts 6:1). Israelite means a member of God's covenant people (Romans 9:4; 11:1). Offspring of Abraham means heir to the promises. These show the rivals were Jewish-Christian, and that they used their roots as credentials. Paul does not deny his Jewishness or call it worthless. He says only that in Christ these credentials are not what makes someone right with God (Philippians 3:7-9). On the "Paul within Judaism" reading, which scholars like Paula Fredriksen hold, Paul remained a Jew all his life; others think that in Christ he stood outside Judaism in important ways.

a: been in more prisons
p: Acts reports only some of these sufferings; the list shows Acts is selective.
b: Before 2 Corinthians was written, Acts reports one imprisonment of Paul (Philippi, Acts 16:23-40), one beating with rods (Philippi), one stoning (Lystra, Acts 14:19), and no shipwreck (Acts 27 comes later). It reports no synagogue lashings at all. So Paul's own list is far longer than Acts. About the end of the first century 1 Clement 5:6 says Paul was in chains seven times. The list is in the style of Stoic philosophers, who listed hardships to show strength of character (John Fitzgerald). Paul's twist is that he lists them to show weakness.
r: Acts 16:22-24; Acts 14:19; Acts 27:41; 1 Clement 5:6; 2 Corinthians 4:8-9; 2 Corinthians 6:4-10; Romans 8:35

a: forty blows less one
p: Jewish courts limited a beating to forty blows; the custom was to give thirty-nine.
b: The limit comes from Deuteronomy: "He may give him forty blows, but no more" (Deuteronomy 25:3). To make sure no one broke the limit by miscounting, the custom was to stop at thirty-nine, as the Mishnah (Makkot 3:10) and Josephus (Antiquities 4.238) report. The beating was a punishment imposed by synagogue authorities (Matthew 10:17; Acts 22:19; 26:11). Five of them mean Paul stayed under the discipline of Jewish communities. Some scholars (the "Paul within Judaism" reading) take this as evidence that Paul kept considering himself part of the Jewish community and was punished as a member, not as an outsider. Others see only that synagogues disciplined him for his message.

a: beaten with rods
p: The rod beatings were Roman punishments; the stoning is probably the one at Lystra.
b: Beating with rods was done by Roman officials (Acts 16:22-23 at Philippi). A Roman citizen should have been spared this; Acts says Paul was a citizen but spoke of it at Philippi only afterward (Acts 16:37). The stoning is probably Acts 14:19, at Lystra, where Paul was dragged out of the town and left for dead. The three shipwrecks are not told in Acts, whose famous shipwreck (Acts 27) comes after this letter. "A night and a day in the open sea" may mean he floated, perhaps on wreckage, until he was rescued.

a: many fasts
p: The Greek word can mean chosen fasting or enforced hunger.
b: The word nēsteia usually means a chosen fast, which Paul and his companions did before choosing leaders (Acts 13:2-3; 14:23). But "hunger and thirst" has just been named, so commentators disagree on whether this means voluntary fasting as a religious practice, or the hunger of someone with no money for food. Both can be true. The line shows that he had neither money nor a patron's table.

a: King Aretas
t: Aretas, Damascus and a rough date
p: King Aretas of the Nabateans gives a rough date to Paul's early life.
b: Aretas IV ruled the Nabatean kingdom (south and east of Judea) from about 9 BC to AD 40. He was the father-in-law whom Herod Antipas insulted by divorcing his daughter, and he defeated Antipas in war (Josephus, Antiquities 18.109-115). How he governed Damascus is unclear: perhaps a Roman emperor gave him control about AD 37-40, in which case the Greek ethnarchēs means a governor under him, or the "ethnarch" was only the head of the Nabatean community in the city. The Plain's "governor" follows the first reading. If the first reading is right, Paul's escape probably falls in the late 30s; on the second it gives no firm date. Acts says "the Jews" watched the gates (Acts 9:23-25), while Paul names the governor; both can be true at once. Martin Hengel, Anna Maria Schwemer and Jerome Murphy-O'Connor discuss this.

a: lowered in a basket
t: A wall, a basket and a missing crown
p: In Rome the first soldier over an enemy wall won a crown; Paul's only wall story is a retreat.
b: The Roman army gave the corona muralis, the "wall crown", to the first soldier over an enemy wall (described by Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 5.6). The idea that Paul closes his list of hardships with this story as a parody of that honor is credited to E. A. Judge and developed by Victor Furnish in his Anchor Bible commentary. It is a suggestion, and not every scholar accepts it. It fits the way the fool's speech turns every boast upside down: the only wall he is known for is the one he went down, in a basket. But Paul himself does not say it.

a: visions and revelations from the Lord
p: The Greek can mean visions given by the Lord or visions of the Lord.
b: Optasiai ("visions") are things seen; apokalypseis ("revelations") are things unveiled. Both are followed by "of the Lord", which can mean the Lord is the giver or the Lord is the one seen. The Plain says "from the Lord" because 12:2-4 describes an experience Paul says he was given. Paul reports other revelations elsewhere: the revelation of Jesus Christ that made him an apostle (Galatians 1:12), the one that sent him to Jerusalem (Galatians 2:2), and visions in Acts (Acts 16:9; 18:9; 22:17-21; 23:11).
r: Galatians 1:12; Galatians 2:2; Acts 16:9; Acts 18:9; Acts 22:17-21; Acts 23:11

a: I know a man in Christ.
p: Paul speaks in the third person, but almost all scholars think he means himself.
b: The reasons for "himself": he is boasting (12:1); the experience is the reason for the thorn (12:7), and the thorn was given to him; and he says he "will not boast" about himself, but about this man (12:5), which is how someone speaks to avoid self-praise. Plutarch's essay on self-praise advises just this kind of distance. Early Christian readers took it as Paul. A few modern scholars read it as another person, or as Paul distancing his ecstatic self from his everyday self, since he contrasts the "man" with "myself" in 12:5. "A man in Christ" is simply a Christian, since Paul's usual phrase for believers is "in Christ".

a: Fourteen years ago
p: Counted from this letter, the experience falls around AD 41-42, a period Acts hardly describes.
b: If 2 Corinthians was written about AD 55-56, fourteen years earlier is around AD 41-42. Paul's call near Damascus was earlier (about AD 33-34), so this is a separate event. Those were years in Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1:21), and probably at Antioch (Acts 11:25-26). Acts tells of no vision then. The temple trance of Acts 22:17-21 happened soon after Paul's first Jerusalem visit, which was too early. So the experience cannot be matched to anything in Acts; the dates also differ by a year or two between scholars. Paul had kept it private for fourteen years.

a: snatched up as far as the third heaven
p: Paul's word means to seize by force; its Latin form gave English the word "rapture".
b: The Greek harpazō means to snatch, as when the Spirit snatched Philip away (Acts 8:39). It is the word used for the believers who will be "caught up" in 1 Thessalonians 4:17. The Latin Bible (Vulgate) translated it rapiemur there and raptum here, and English "rapture" comes from that Latin. The same verb in two passages does not mean they describe the same event: this one is a private visionary experience of one man, the other a gathering of all believers at Christ's return. Paul adds that he cannot tell whether his own body went along (12:2-3).
orig: ἁρπαγέντα ... ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ (harpagenta ... heōs tritou ouranou)

a: third heaven
t: Comparison only: ascents to heaven in Jewish writings
p: Jewish writings of Paul's era and later describe journeys through layered heavens, a useful comparison.
b: Ancient Jews and others thought of several layers of heaven. 2 Enoch (a Jewish work that survives in Slavonic) puts Paradise in the third heaven (2 Enoch 8), and the Life of Adam and Eve places Adam's soul in the third heaven (Apocalypse of Moses 37:5). The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs have seven heavens in most copies (Testament of Levi 2-3). The later rabbinic and mystical traditions tell of four sages who "entered the Pardes", the Paradise (Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah 14b), and still later Hekhalot texts such as 3 Enoch describe journeys through heavenly palaces. The writings named here (2 Enoch, the Life of Adam and Eve, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, 3 Enoch) are in no church's Bible, and their dates are uncertain, with 3 Enoch much later than Paul. These are comparisons, not sources: most are later than Paul or cannot be dated, and none says Paul used them. Alan Segal and C. R. A. Morray-Jones think Paul belongs in this stream; Martha Himmelfarb surveys it.
r: 2 Enoch 8; Apocalypse of Moses 37:5; Testament of Levi 2-3; Hagigah 14b; 3 Enoch; Psalm 148:4; Deuteronomy 10:14

a: whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know
t: In the body or out of it?
p: Paul is unsure whether his whole self travelled or only his spirit; he does not rule either out.
b: Paul's uncertainty shows that he thought it possible for a person to be taken up while the body stayed behind, or to be taken body and all. Both appear in Scripture: Ezekiel was lifted "by the Spirit" in visions (Ezekiel 8:3), and Philip was carried bodily (Acts 8:39). John writes that he was "in the Spirit" when he saw heaven opened (Revelation 4:1-2). The line is also part of Paul's wider teaching about the body and what lies outside it (2 Corinthians 5:1-10). Paul's "I do not know" is a model of restraint: God knows, and that is enough for him.

a: Paradise
p: A Persian word for a walled garden, used by Greek-speaking Jews for the Garden of Eden.
b: The word comes from an old Persian term for an enclosed park. The Septuagint uses paradeisos for the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8) and in Ezekiel (28:13; 31:8). By the first century it was also a name for a place of the righteous near God. Jesus tells the man beside him on the cross that he will be "in Paradise" (Luke 23:43), and in Revelation the tree of life stands "in the Paradise of God" (Revelation 2:7). Paul places Paradise in the third heaven: for him heaven and Paradise are one place or two ways of describing it. Augustine took the third heaven to be a kind of seeing without images, the highest of three kinds of vision (Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 12).

a: unspeakable words, words no human being is allowed to say
t: Words that cannot or may not be spoken
p: The Greek can mean that the words are beyond speech or that speaking them is forbidden.
b: Arrēta rhēmata means "unspeakable words". The next phrase uses exon, which can mean "it is permitted" or "it is possible". So the words are either forbidden to repeat or beyond human language to repeat. Paul's silence also makes a point about the fool's speech: the one thing he might have bragged about, he refuses to describe. He has chosen to boast of his weaknesses instead (12:5, 9). Later Christian writers filled the gap with speculation, which Paul does not do.
orig: ἄρρητα ῥήματα ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι

a: a thorn was given to me in the flesh
t: A thorn, a stake, or a splinter
p: The Greek word means something sharp and painful; what it stood for is the most debated question in 2 Corinthians.
b: Skolops can mean a thorn, a splinter, or a stake. "Was given" is a passive that Jews used for God's act: God gave it, though Satan's messenger delivered it. "In the flesh" may mean in the body, or it may mean "for the flesh", for his human weakness. The Septuagint uses the word for troubles that opponents cause: "thorns in your eyes" for Canaanites left in the land (Numbers 33:55) and "a thorn of bitterness" for hostile neighbors (Ezekiel 28:24). The readings of what the thorn was are set out in this chapter's deep dive and on the topic page; the passage does not say which is right.
orig: ἐδόθη μοι σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί (edothē moi skolops tē sarki)

a: a messenger of Satan, to beat me
p: Satan delivers the blow, but God gives it for a good end, as in Job.
b: "Messenger" (angelos) usually means "angel" but just means "one sent". So the phrase may name a demon, a human enemy, or an illness thought of as an attack. "To beat" (kolaphizō) means to strike with the fist, as the guards did to Jesus (Mark 14:65), and Paul uses it of his own treatment (1 Corinthians 4:11). The tense means the blows keep coming. In Job, Satan can only strike within the limits God sets (Job 1:12; 2:6). Paul similarly says in 1 Corinthians 5:5 that a man may be handed to Satan for his good. Here the purpose is Paul's own humility.

a: three times I begged the Lord
p: Paul's three requests echo Jesus's three prayers in Gethsemane.
b: Jesus prayed three times in Gethsemane that the cup might pass, and the answer was that it would not (Mark 14:32-42). Paul's three requests, and a refusal that is also a promise, follow the same shape. "The Lord" here is Jesus, as 12:9 shows ("the power of Christ"). The answer of 12:9 is also the form of a prophetic oracle: God's answer to a prayer of lament, as in the psalms where a priest or prophet speaks God's word back (for example Psalm 12:5). Paul thus presents himself as praying like Jesus, and as answered like a psalmist.

a: "My grace is enough for you. Power is made complete in weakness."
p: The answer is given in a tense that means it still stands.
b: The words "he has said" are in the perfect tense: the Lord spoke, and what he said still holds. "Is enough" (arkei) means suffices; "made complete" (teleitai) means brought to its goal. Grace here is not a feeling but God's active help. The answer does not remove the thorn. It changes what the thorn means. Paul's reading of the answer is that he can "boast" of weakness because there Christ's power becomes visible. In Corinth, where strength meant status, it was a hard teaching.
orig: ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου· ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται

a: set up its tent over me
p: The verb is used nowhere else in the New Testament; it may echo God's presence in the tent of meeting.
b: Episkēnoō means to pitch a tent upon or dwell over. In Exodus the cloud covered the tent of meeting and the glory of the LORD filled it (Exodus 40:34-35). In John, the Word "pitched his tent" among us (John 1:14, the verb skēnoō). It is possible that Paul wants his weak body to be the place where Christ's power stays, as the glory stayed in the tent. This is a suggestion; Paul does not quote Exodus. In 5:1-4 he calls the body a tent as well.

a: when I am weak, then I am strong
p: Paul does not praise suffering for its own sake; he says weakness is where Christ's power shows.
b: The line is a paradox, not a program. "Weak" means lacking the resources people use to impress: money, speaking skill, health, status. In that emptiness, Christ's power can be seen. It is based on the cross: Christ "was crucified out of weakness, but he lives by God's power" (13:4). Martin Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (1518) made this pattern the mark of a "theologian of the cross", who finds God where the world sees only weakness (thesis 21). Paul's wording has been misused to urge people to stay in abuse; the passage is about Paul's choice, as a messenger, to accept hardship he could not remove.

a: The signs that mark an apostle
t: Signs, wonders and acts of power
p: Paul claims all three kinds of miracle among the Corinthians but spends no time on them.
b: The three terms (sēmeia, terata, dynameis) are used together of Jesus's own works (Acts 2:22) and of the works that backed up the apostles' message (Romans 15:18-19; Hebrews 2:4). The Greek says "the signs of the apostle" (with "the"), which may mean "of a true apostle", "of the apostle I am", or what the rivals called such signs. Paul puts "complete endurance" first, since he thought patient suffering was the primary mark of an apostle (6:4-10). He does not describe any miracle in Corinth: Acts 18 mentions none. Churches still disagree about whether such signs go on today; see the card.

a: Forgive me this wrong!
p: Paul jokes about the "wrong" of not charging them.
b: The joke has a point. The Corinthians took Paul's refusal of pay as an insult (see the note at 11:7). He is asking sarcastic forgiveness for not letting them be his patrons. A serious principle is under it: Paul will not be a client of a church he is trying to correct, since pay would give them leverage over him.

a: this is the third time I am ready to come to you
p: The third visit is the next one; the second was the painful visit.
b: Paul's first visit founded the church (Acts 18:1-18). The second, apparently brief and painful, is the visit that left him "in tears" (2:1; 13:2). The third is the one he is now preparing (13:1). Another reading says the Greek means "for the third time I am ready", that is, he was twice ready before but delayed (1:15-16, the changed plan), so there may have been only two actual visits before this. 13:2 may speak of a "second visit" as past, which would favor the first reading, but the Greek of 13:2 can also be read another way (see the note there), so it does not settle the count. The visits are not recorded in Acts; they are known only from Paul's letters.

a: Children are not expected to put money aside for their parents, but parents for their children.
p: Paul speaks of ordinary custom: young children do not support parents, but parents provide for them.
b: This does not cancel the duty of adult children to support aged parents (Exodus 20:12; Mark 7:9-13). Paul describes the ordinary pattern of a household with young children, and uses it for his relationship to Corinth. He has already called himself their father (1 Corinthians 4:14-15). Later, to the Thessalonians, he likens himself to both a nursing mother and a father (1 Thessalonians 2:7, 11).

a: I caught you with a trick
p: Some in Corinth suspected that Paul took nothing for himself but used the collection to profit.
b: The accusation is likely that Paul took no money openly but was secretly enriched through the collection for Jerusalem, which Titus and others were gathering (8:6, 16-24; 9:3-5). Paul's reply is a string of questions that expect a "no": Titus was clean, and they walked in the same steps. This is why chapters 8 and 9 are so careful about having named, trusted men handle the money (8:20-21). The collection mattered to Paul as a sign of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers (Romans 15:25-31; Galatians 2:10). The words "some say" are the Plain's own addition to show that Paul is quoting a charge; the Greek names no speaker.
r: 2 Corinthians 8:6; 2 Corinthians 8:16-24; 2 Corinthians 9:3-5; Romans 15:25-31; Galatians 2:10; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4

a: the brother
p: An unnamed companion of Titus; the letter does not say who he was.
b: Titus is known from several places in this letter (2:13; 7:6-16; 8:6, 16-24). Chapter 8 mentions two brothers who went with him: one "famous in the gospel" (8:18) and another tested (8:22). The same "brother" may be the first of those. Later writers guessed Luke, Barnabas or Apollos; none of these is stated in the text, and the identity is unknown. See the notes at 8:18 in the part of this book that covers chapter 8.

a: strife, jealousy, tempers, rivalry, backbiting, whispering, swelled heads and unrest
p: The eight words describe a church at war with itself; they look like a political quarrel, not private vices.
b: Most of these words appear in other Pauline lists: strife and jealousy in 1 Corinthians 3:3, and tempers, rivalry and jealousy in Galatians 5:20. In practice, the picture is of groups tearing each other down: factions and bad-mouthing, whispers behind backs, and inflated egos (physiōseis, the word for "puffed up" in 1 Corinthians 4:6, 18-19). The "unrest" or disorder (akatastasiai) is a word for civil confusion. So what Paul fears on arrival is a church divided by rivalry, which is the same problem as 1 Corinthians 1:10-12.

a: the uncleanness, the sexual immorality and the shameless living
p: Paul fears some have not repented of sexual sins he addressed in the first letter.
b: The three nouns are akatharsia (uncleanness), porneia (sexual immorality) and aselgeia (living without restraint or shame). 1 Corinthians 5 and 6 had already dealt with sexual wrongdoing in Corinth. It seems that some had not changed. "Mourn" is the response Paul expected of the whole church when the man living with his father's wife was tolerated (1 Corinthians 5:2). The verse also shows Paul expects to be shamed ("humbled") by the church's failure, as a father might be.

a: "Every matter will stand on the word of two witnesses or of three."
p: Paul quotes the rule of Deuteronomy for settling a charge.
b: The rule is Deuteronomy 19:15: "A matter is to stand on the word of two witnesses or on the word of three witnesses." It prevents one person's word from convicting anyone. Jesus applies it to a church dispute (Matthew 18:16), and the New Testament uses it elsewhere (John 8:17; 1 Timothy 5:19). Commentators differ on how Paul applies it. Some think he means a formal hearing, with proper evidence, before he punishes anyone. Others think the "witnesses" are his repeated warnings or visits (the second visit, this letter and the coming visit). Either way, he is promising fairness, not a rush to judgment.

a: I will not spare anyone
p: Paul does not say what the punishment would be.
b: The threat is not explained. Readers have thought of exclusion from the community (1 Corinthians 5:5, 13), a miracle of judgment like the blinding of Elymas (Acts 13:11) or the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), or simply a stern public rebuke. Paul in 1 Corinthians 4:21 asked whether he should come "with a rod". Here he states the aim: building up, not tearing down (13:10).

a: as I did on my second visit
t: A second visit past, or "as if present the second time"?
p: The Greek can mean "as when I was there the second time" or "as if I were there the second time".
b: The Greek is hōs paron to deuteron kai apon nyn. It can mean "as when I was present the second time, and now I am absent" (the Plain's reading, which counts a past second visit, so that the visit now planned is the third). It can also mean "as if I were present the second time, though I am absent now" (the sense behind the KJV), in which case Paul may be speaking of a second visit that is still ahead, and the count of visits could be two, not three. The Plain keeps the first reading, but the choice is a judgment, and the note at 12:14 shows how much depends on it.

a: proof that Christ speaks in me
p: A family of Greek words about testing appears five times in these verses.
b: Dokimē ("proof"), dokimazō ("to test"), dokimos ("approved, passing the test") and adokimos ("failing the test") form a chain through 13:3-7 and back to 10:18. The Corinthians demand proof that Christ speaks in Paul. He turns the demand around: they should test themselves. The word-play is hard to keep in English, so the Plain says "pass the test" or "fail the test" each time. The same word describes metal that is tested in the fire and found genuine.

a: he was crucified out of weakness
p: Christ's weakness and his life by God's power are the pattern Paul claims for himself.
b: The preposition ek ("out of") is a little odd: it can mean "from the condition of weakness" or "because of weakness". Either way, the cross is the deepest weakness. Paul had already said that the cross is "the weakness of God" that is stronger than human strength (1 Corinthians 1:25). The next lines copy the pattern: we are weak in him, and we will live with him, by God's power, toward you. The sentence also says what 12:9-10 means by weakness. For the hymn behind this, compare Philippians 2:6-11.

a: Check yourselves to see whether you are in the faith.
p: Paul tells the Corinthians to test themselves instead of testing him.
b: "The faith" here is the Christian message and the trust that answers it. The Corinthians want proof that Christ speaks through Paul; Paul says the proof is that Christ is in them, and that Christ was made known to them through Paul. Whether "in you" means in each person or among the church is debated: the Greek en hymin allows both (Galatians 4:19; Romans 8:10; Colossians 1:27). Paul's call for self-examination is similar to the one before the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:28). The warning is about the church's whole standing, not a private checklist; the card on assurance shows how churches have used the verse.
orig: ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει

a: your restoration
p: The word is used of mending broken nets and putting a person right.
b: Katartisis comes from a verb meaning to put in order or mend. It is used for the fishermen "mending" their nets (Mark 1:19), for gently "restoring" someone who has fallen (Galatians 6:1), and for making a body fit to work (Ephesians 4:12). Paul uses the same verb as a command in 13:11, "be restored". It tells us what his goal is: not to win an argument but to put the church back in working order.

a: Take comfort.
p: The verb parakaleō carries four meanings, and the letter has used all of them.
b: The word parakaleō means to call alongside: to comfort, to encourage, to appeal to, or to ask. In 1:3-7 it occurs about ten times, mostly as "comfort". Here it is a passive or middle verb, which can mean "be comforted", "be encouraged", "listen to my appeal" or "encourage one another". The Plain says "Take comfort", the sense that matches the start of the letter. The whole list in 13:11 is a short summary of what a healthy church does.

a: a holy kiss
p: A greeting kiss among believers marked them as a family, and later became part of worship.
b: Kissing on the cheek was a common greeting between family and friends. Paul asks for it in several letters (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26), and Peter calls it a "kiss of love" (1 Peter 5:14). Here it comes right after the call to peace and the warning of discipline, as a sign of restored friendship. By the mid-second century Justin Martyr describes the kiss exchanged after the prayers, before the bread and wine (First Apology 65). The "sign of peace" in Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant services descends from it.

a: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.
p: A blessing that names Jesus, God and the Spirit; its verse number differs by edition.
b: Numbering: English Bibles number this verse 13:14. Greek editions put it at 13:13, because they treat the greeting of the saints in English 13:13 as the second half of 13:12. The words are the same. Wording: koinōnia can be "fellowship" (the friendship the Spirit creates among believers), "sharing" or "participation" in the Spirit. The Greek "of the Holy Spirit" can mean either. In Acts 2:42 the Plain says "the fellowship". Meaning: This is the only place in Paul's letters where the Lord Jesus, God and the Spirit are named in one blessing, in that order: Christ, the Father, the Spirit. See the card for how churches read it and the topic on the Trinity. The blessing is used to open the Mass, the Orthodox Divine Liturgy's central prayer, and many Protestant services.
orig: ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἡ κοινωνία τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος
